407.title: Eat, drink, don't waste
407.hook: eat and drink but don't be wasteful (7:31)
407.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to avoid israf in food, water and money; some keep the hadith of thirds in mind at meals, and teachers often point to the small amount of water the Prophet used for wudu.

segments.voice: Yesterday: libas, the garment, and the garment of piety. Your line was the best clothing is inside. Today, five verses later, from the closet to the kitchen.

Open almost any fridge on a Sunday night. Half a bag of spinach gone slimy. The rice nobody wanted. A yogurt two weeks past its date. Food that was paid for goes in the bin, and more gets bought. At the other end of the scale, a hadith shows the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ washing for prayer with about a double handful of water. Between those two pictures sits a short line in surah seven that sounds almost too simple to need saying.
screen: `THE SUNDAY NIGHT FRIDGE.` → `A DOUBLE HANDFUL OF WATER.` → `TOO SIMPLE TO NEED SAYING.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “O Children of Adam! Look to your adornment at every place of worship, and eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals.” Two halves. The first is about clothing again. A report in Sahih Muslim explains why: before Islam, some people circled the Ka'bah unclothed, and this verse told them to come to worship dressed, even dressed well. The second half is about the table. Eat. Drink. Enjoy it; the next verse asks who could forbid the good things Allah has provided. But don't commit israf. The root s-r-f means to go past the limit, to overshoot: israf is excess, beyond what's needed. The Qur'an has a separate word, tabdhir, in surah seventeen, for scattering wealth away on nothing, and it's sharp about both. A hadith in Tirmidhi gives a measure for eating: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink, a third for breath. And Bukhari records that the Prophet made wudu with a mudd, roughly what two cupped hands hold, and bathed with only a few times that. Teachers take it as a lesson: enough is a real amount, and you can find it. The verse doesn't say eat less than you need, or never enjoy food. It says eat, drink, and stop at enough. The opposite of israf isn't hunger. It's the right amount, used well.
screen: `DRESSED FOR WORSHIP.` · `EAT AND DRINK — ENJOY IT.` · `ISRAF — PAST THE LIMIT.` · `A THIRD, A THIRD, A THIRD.` · then, large: `BE NOT PRODIGAL.`

segments.voice: Walk through the day ahead in your mind and look, without judging, for the leaks: water running while you brush your teeth, food that will go bad, a light on in an empty room, a purchase you don't need. Then picture your next meal, eaten slowly, ending at enough, with a little room left for breath.
Israf. Excess, going past the limit. Surah seven: eat and drink, but don't be wasteful, for Allah does not love the wasteful. Today's word.
Your line: enough, no waste. The good things are a gift to enjoy. Day four hundred seven.

408.title: Humbly and in secret
408.hook: call on your Lord humbly and privately, with fear and hope (7:55–56)
408.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a, personal supplication, at any time and in any language, often quietly after the prayer or in prostration; teachers cite 7:55 for keeping it humble and low-voiced.

segments.voice: Yesterday: israf, going past the limit. Your line was enough, no waste. Today, a limit of another kind: how loud to be when you call on God.

On a journey with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, his companions climbed a hill and, the way travelers do, shouted Allahu akbar into the valley at the top of their lungs. A report in Bukhari says he told them, gently, to take it easy on themselves. You're not calling someone deaf, he said, or someone far away. You're calling one who hears, and who is near. Grown men, mid-shout, lowering their voices. Surah seven, verse fifty-five, says the same thing as a command.
screen: `SHOUTING INTO THE VALLEY.` → `NOT DEAF, NOT FAR AWAY.` → `ONE WHO HEARS, AND IS NEAR.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Lo! He loveth not aggressors.” Two Arabic words carry the manner. Tadarru'an: humbly, with the pleading of someone who really needs something. Khufyatan: hidden, privately, under your breath. The prophet Zakariyya does exactly this in surah nineteen: an old man calling his Lord in a secret call, asking quietly for a child. The verse then warns that Allah doesn't love those who overstep. Commentators gave examples of overstepping in du'a: shouting, praying for something harmful, or demanding absurd detail. A report in Abu Dawud tells of a companion who heard his son ask for the white palace on the right side of paradise, and told him to ask simply for paradise. The next verse adds two more words: call on Him in fear and hope, khawfan wa tama'an. Not only fear, which can crush; not only hope, which can turn careless. Both, like two wings of a bird, as some scholars put it. And the verse ends: the mercy of Allah is near to those who do good. Near: the same thing the Prophet said on the hill. In this teaching, a quiet du'a needs no audience, no microphone, no perfect Arabic. It can happen at a red light, in the shower, at two in the morning. The verse asks only that it be humble, and that it be yours.
screen: `TADARRU' — HUMBLY, PLEADING.` · `KHUFYAH — HIDDEN, UNDER THE BREATH.` · `DON'T OVERSTEP.` · `FEAR AND HOPE, TWO WINGS.` · then, large: `HUMBLY AND IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Let your voice go quiet, even inside your head, and name plainly one thing you actually need: health for someone, a way through a problem, a softer heart. If you pray, make a du'a for it now in your own words, under your breath; if you don't, hold that need quietly, with a little fear and a little hope.
Tadarru'an, humbly, the way someone pleads when they truly need something. Call on your Lord that way, and in secret, in fear and hope, for His mercy is near. Today's word.
Your line: humbly, in secret. The One you're calling hears, and is near. Four hundred eight days now.

409.title: Hud and 'Ad
409.hook: Hud warns the builders of high towers, and the wind comes (7:65–72)
409.howItsDone: Muslims honor Hud as a prophet sent to the Arabian people of 'Ad; surah eleven bears his name, and teachers read his story as a warning against trusting strength and wealth instead of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tadarru'an, humbly and in secret. Your line was humbly, in secret. Today, surah seven begins a run of prophets, one people at a time.

Cities race each other for the tallest building, and boast when they win. Glass towers, stone walls, a bigger house, a bigger bank balance, a big following. Building isn't wrong. But sometimes people build not to shelter anyone, only to feel that nothing can touch them. The Qur'an tells of an ancient Arabian people called 'Ad, famous for their strength and their building, and of a man from among them sent to warn them. His name was Hud.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TALLEST BUILDING.` → `BUILT TO FEEL UNTOUCHABLE.` → `A PEOPLE CALLED 'AD.`

segments.voice: Surah seven, verse sixty-five, introduces him simply: to 'Ad, their brother Hud. Not a stranger; one of their own. His message is the one Nuh brought just before him: my people, worship Allah, you have no god but Him. He reminds them that Allah made them successors after the people of Nuh and gave them great stature and strength. The chiefs call him a fool and a liar, and say they won't leave what their fathers worshipped. Other surahs fill in the picture. In surah twenty-six, Hud asks: do you build a landmark on every high place, just for show, and fortresses, as if you'll live forever? In surah forty-one, they boast: who is mightier than us in strength? Surah eighty-nine names their city Iram, of the lofty pillars. Then the end. Surah forty-six says they saw a cloud coming toward their valleys and said, this cloud will bring us rain. It wasn't rain. Surah sixty-nine calls it a furious, roaring wind, sent against them for seven nights and eight days, until they lay like the hollow trunks of palm trees. Surah seven says simply that Allah saved Hud and those with him, and cut off the rest. Where were they? Surah forty-six places them at al-Ahqaf, the sand dunes, which commentators set in southern Arabia; beyond that, the sources don't say for certain. The lesson doesn't need the map. Towers, pillars, strength: none of it was safety.
screen: `THEIR BROTHER HUD.` · `A LANDMARK ON EVERY HIGH PLACE.` · `A CLOUD THEY THOUGHT WAS RAIN.` · `SEVEN NIGHTS, EIGHT DAYS.` · then, large: `TOWERS AREN'T SAFETY.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly what you build to feel strong: savings, a title, a reputation, a body at the gym, the people who'd take your side. None of these is bad, so pick one and hold it in mind. Then ask what would still hold you up if it were gone tomorrow, and stay with whatever answer comes, even a quiet one.
Hud. A prophet sent to his own people, the great builders of ancient Arabia, 'Ad, who trusted their strength until the wind came. Today's word.
Your line: towers aren't safety. Strength was never the shelter. That's day four hundred nine.

410.title: Salih and the she-camel
410.hook: Thamud are given a she-camel as a sign and told to let her graze (7:73–79)
410.howItsDone: Muslims honor Salih as a prophet sent to Thamud; his story is taught alongside hadith on kindness to animals, and teachers recall the reports about the Prophet passing al-Hijr.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hud and 'Ad, and the wind. Your line was towers aren't safety. Today, the next people in surah seven, and the next brother sent to them.

In northwest Arabia, near the town of al-Ula, enormous tombs are carved straight into sandstone cliffs, their doorways cut like temple fronts. Muslim tradition has long linked this region, al-Hijr, with the people of Thamud. Archaeologists date the tombs standing there now to the Nabataeans, a later people. But the Qur'an says Thamud, too, carved homes out of mountains. And it tells of a sign sent to them that wasn't a wall or a tower at all. It was an animal. A she-camel.
screen: `TOMBS CARVED INTO CLIFFS.` → `AL-HIJR, AND THAMUD.` → `A SIGN THAT WAS AN ANIMAL.`

segments.voice: Verse seventy-three: to Thamud, their brother Salih. Same message as Hud: worship Allah, you have no god but Him. Then he points to a sign: this is the she-camel of Allah. Let her eat in Allah's earth, and don't touch her with harm, or a painful punishment will take you. The Arabic is naqat Allah, the camel of God, a phrase that gives an ordinary animal enormous dignity. Surah twenty-six adds that the water was to be shared: a day for her to drink, and a day for the people. The test was almost too simple. Leave her alone. Share the well. Salih reminds them of their blessings: Allah made them successors after 'Ad, with plains for palaces and mountains to carve into homes. The proud chiefs mock the poorer people who believed. Then, verse seventy-seven, they hamstring the she-camel and say to Salih, bring on what you threaten. Surah ninety-one says it was done by the most wretched of them, while the people went along. The earthquake took them, and morning found them fallen in their homes. When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ later passed through al-Hijr on the way to Tabuk, Bukhari reports he told his companions not to enter the dwellings of those punished except in tears. Elsewhere, hadith tell of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and a woman punished for starving a cat. In this tradition, how people treat an animal is never a small thing.

segments.voice: Picture an animal you'll likely cross today, a pigeon on the sidewalk, a neighbor's dog, a cat in an alley, a bee at a window, going about its business. Then picture yourself simply letting it be, not chasing, shooing or swatting, maybe leaving a little water out, and hold that picture of an animal left in peace.
Salih. A prophet sent to Thamud, and a sign, a she-camel, that asked only to be left in peace and given her share of water. Today's word.
Your line: leave her to graze. The whole test was one animal and a shared well. Until tomorrow.

411.title: Shu'ayb and the scales
411.hook: Shu'ayb tells Madyan to give full measure and not cheat people of their things (7:85)
411.howItsDone: Muslim jurists treat honest weights and measures as a religious duty, and Islamic cities historically had a market inspector, the muhtasib, who checked scales; many Muslim traders cite Shu'ayb and surah eighty-three.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Salih and the she-camel. Your line was leave her to graze. Today, the third brother in a row, and this time the trouble is in the marketplace.
screen: `SALIH AND THE SHE-CAMEL — LEAVE HER TO GRAZE.`

segments.voice: A bag of chips that's mostly air. A gas pump off by a fraction. An invoice padded with an hour nobody worked. A shop scale nudged so a kilo is a little less than a kilo. Each one is small and easy to deny, and across thousands of customers they add up to someone getting rich on a sliver from everyone. The Qur'an tells of a whole town that ran on slivers, and of the prophet sent to them, Shu'ayb.
screen: `A BAG THAT'S MOSTLY AIR.` → `A SCALE, NUDGED.` → `A TOWN THAT RAN ON SLIVERS.`

segments.voice: Verse eighty-five: to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb. Madyan was a trading people; many place them in northwest Arabia, near the Gulf of Aqaba. Shu'ayb begins with the same call as Hud and Salih: worship Allah, you have no god but Him. Then, in Pickthall's words: “give full measure and full weight and wrong not mankind in their goods.” The word for weight, mizan, is the balance scale itself. And their goods is ashya'ahum, literally their things: don't shortchange people in anything that's theirs. Don't spread corruption in the land after it has been set right. The next verse warns them against lurking on every road to threaten travelers. The town's leaders answer with an ultimatum: leave, Shu'ayb, you and everyone who believes with you, or come back to our ways. His reply is a short question: even if we hate them? He won't go back, and he asks God to judge between them with truth. Notice what the town is defending: not only its gods, but a way of doing business that worked very well for the people at the top. Some commentators identified Shu'ayb with the father-in-law of Musa; many disagreed, and the Qur'an doesn't say. The end of Madyan, verse ninety-one, is the earthquake again. But the warning outlived the town. A whole short surah, eighty-three, opens with woe to those who give short measure. Fair weight is no footnote in this tradition. It sits right next to worship.

segments.voice: Think of the places you measure something out for others: the hours on a timesheet, the change at a register, the effort on a group project, the split of a dinner bill, the slice of cake you cut for someone else. Find one place where you've been giving a little short, picture giving it full, maybe a touch more, and notice how that feels.

412.title: Let me see You
412.hook: Musa asks to see Allah, the mountain crumbles, and he falls fainting, then repents (7:143)
412.carry: the mountain could not bear it
412.howItsDone: Muslims honor Musa as kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to; the scene at the mountain is often recited and taught as a picture of longing for God, and of His majesty beyond what creation can bear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shu'ayb and the scales. Your line was full measure. Today, surah seven reaches Musa, and a request nobody expects.

Musa has been called from beside a fire, has stood before Pharaoh, has watched the sea split. Now Allah sets him an appointment: thirty nights on the mountain, completed with ten more, forty in all. He goes up alone, and there Allah speaks to him. That's why Muslims give Musa the title kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to. It might seem like enough. Musa, standing in that conversation, asks for one thing more.
screen: `FORTY NIGHTS ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `KALIMULLAH — THE ONE ALLAH SPOKE TO.` → `ONE THING MORE.`

segments.voice: Verse one-forty-three. Musa says: rabbi arini anzur ilayk. My Lord, show me, so that I may look at You. A request made out of longing, not arrogance. The answer comes, in Pickthall's words: “Thou wilt not see Me, but gaze upon the mountain!” If it stays firm in its place, then you will see Me. Then Allah reveals His glory to the mountain, and the mountain is crushed, made level, turned to dust. Musa falls down unconscious. When he comes to, his first words are: glory be to You. I turn to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers. What does he repent of? Some commentators say it wasn't a sin, exactly, but asking for more than a human being can bear. The text doesn't scold the longing. It shows its size with a mountain that couldn't hold it. Jews and Christians know a related scene in Exodus, where Moses asks to see God's glory and is told no one can see God's face and live; each tradition tells it in its own way. And the swoon echoes later. A hadith in Bukhari says that on the Day of Resurrection, when people fall unconscious, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ will be the first to wake, and he'll find Musa already there, holding the side of the Throne. The Prophet said he didn't know whether Musa woke first, or was spared that swoon because of the one on the mountain. Musa's longing, it seems, wasn't wasted.

413.title: "Am I not your Lord?"
413.hook: the souls of Adam's children are asked, am I not your Lord, and say, yes (7:172)
413.howItsDone: Muslims teach 7:172 as the primordial covenant (al-mithaq) and link it to the fitrah, the natural disposition toward God; Sufi poets, especially in Persian, call it the day of Alast.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arini, let me see You, and the mountain. Your line was the mountain could not bear it. A week ends today: no waste, a quiet du'a, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Musa on the mountain. Now a question older than all of them.
screen: `ARINI — THE MOUNTAIN COULD NOT BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: A song heard for the first time that seems already known. A street never walked before that somehow says, I know this. Persian poets had a name for an older version of that feeling: the day of Alast. They meant a moment before anyone was born, when every human soul heard a single question and gave a single answer. They took it from one verse in surah seven, and Alast is simply the first word of that question in Arabic.
screen: `A SONG YOU'VE ALWAYS KNOWN.` → `THE DAY OF ALAST.` → `ONE QUESTION, ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Verse one-seventy-two says your Lord brought out from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify about themselves. Then the question, in Pickthall's words: “Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily. We testify.” In Arabic: alastu bi-rabbikum? Qalu bala. The verse gives the reason: so that no one can say on the Day of Resurrection, we didn't know about this. Scholars call this al-mithaq, the covenant, from a root meaning to bind firmly, like a rope tied tight; the word appears in the verses just before. What exactly happened? Muslim scholars read it two main ways. Some, citing a hadith in which Umar asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about this verse, take it as a real event: every soul drawn out and asked, before the world began. Others read it as a picture of human nature itself, the fitrah: every person made with knowledge of their Lord built in, the testimony written into who they are. Both readings agree on the most striking part. In this telling, faith isn't something foreign added later. It's remembering. Sufi poets took this up. Rumi wrote of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, crying out to go home, and some readers hear in that the soul longing for the day it said yes. The Qur'an's own word for the answer is tiny: bala. Yes.
screen: `ALASTU BI-RABBIKUM?` · `QALU BALA — THEY SAID, YES.` · `AN EVENT, OR HUMAN NATURE?` · `FAITH AS REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `WE SAID YES.`

segments.voice: Imagine, just for a moment, that before your first breath you were asked a question and you answered; you don't have to decide what you believe about it, just sit inside the picture. Then, if it fits, let the word bala, yes, pass through your mind on one quiet out-breath, and if it doesn't, notice what in you wants to say yes to something larger.
Mithaq. The covenant: the firm pledge of 7:172, when the children of Adam were asked, am I not your Lord, and said, yes. Today's word.
Your line: we said yes. A familiar feeling can be a small remembering. Four hundred thirteen days now.
